Displeased
dĭs-plēzd'
v. (offended, made angry — used of God at David's sin and Israel's complaining, of Jonah at God's mercy, and of Christ at those who kept children away)
From Old French desplaisir, from Latin displicere, from dis-, apart, and placere, to please. In the KJV it renders Hebrew ra'a' be'eyne, to be evil in the eyes of, and Greek aganakteo, to be indignant.

Biblical Definition

Displeased is a quiet word for a serious thing, and the KJV uses it at four moments worth setting side by side. Twice it describes God. At the end of the chapter in which David took Bathsheba and had her husband killed, after the mourning, the marriage, and the birth, the writer adds one flat sentence: “But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (2Sa 11:27) — the whole affair had been managed to everyone's satisfaction, and heaven had not been consulted. And in the wilderness: “when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled” (Num 11:1) — grumbling is not a small sin, and fire fell in the uttermost parts of the camp. Once it describes a prophet displeased with God: “But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry” (Jon 4:1) — angry that Nineveh repented and was spared, which he had suspected all along would happen. And once it describes the Lord Jesus: “when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Mar 10:14). It is the only place the Gospels use the word of Him, and the occasion was disciples turning away children.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines displease as to offend, to make angry in a slight degree, to disgust, and displeased as offended, disgusted, or vexed.

expand to see more

DISPLEASE, v.t. To offend; to make angry, sometimes in a slight degree.

To disgust; to excite aversion in; as, sour things displease the taste.

To offend, as by an act contrary to the will or command of another.

DISPLEASED, pp. Offended; disgusted; vexed; provoked.

It is used of the Supreme Being after the manner of men, to signify his holy displeasure at sin.

Key Scripture

2Sa 11:27 — "And when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house, and she became his wife, and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD."

Num 11:1 — "And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp."

Jon 4:1 — "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry."

Mar 10:14 — "But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God."

Modern Corruption

Divine displeasure is either denied outright, as unworthy of a loving God, or reduced to a human mood; Scripture speaks of it plainly while the church confesses that God is without passions.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors gather around this word. The first says a God of love is never displeased, and treats the language of wrath as primitive residue. The second reads the language flatly and makes God a being of fluctuating moods who is upset and then consoled. The Reformed confession holds a narrower and better path. The 1689 Confession says God is “without body, parts, or passions” — He is not acted upon from outside, He does not swing from calm to fury, His displeasure at sin is not a disturbance that comes over Him. And yet it is entirely real: it is the eternal, settled, unchanging opposition of a holy nature to what is contrary to it, expressed in Scripture in language we can bear. The theological term is anthropopathism, and it is not a way of explaining the wrath away. It is a way of saying that God's displeasure is more certain than ours, not less, because it never varies with His temper.

The second thing here is the object of the only displeasure the Gospels attribute to the Lord Jesus. Not the crowds, not the Romans, not even the man with the withered hand's accusers — there He is grieved and angry, and the word is different. Here, in Mar 10:14, He is much displeased with His own disciples for keeping children away from Him, and He answers with a command and a doctrine: suffer them to come, forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of God. Churches that make no room for children, and homes that treat catechising as optional, should sit with that verse a while. And note what David and the disciples have in common: both had arranged matters sensibly, and both had made an arrangement heaven disliked.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin displicere, to displease; Hebrew yera' be'eyne, to be evil in the eyes of; charah 'aph (H2734 + H639), the anger kindled; Greek aganakteo (G23), to be indignant.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to be evil, displeasing; the idiom is literally “it was evil in the eyes of the LORD”.

Hebrew charah (H2734) — to burn, be kindled; used of anger, as in Num 11:1.

Hebrew 'aph (H639) — the nostril, and so anger; the Hebrew pictures wrath as hard breathing.

Greek aganakteo (G23) — to be indignant, much displeased; the word in Mar 10:14.

Greek orge (G3709) — settled wrath, as distinct from thumos, the boiling-over kind; God's wrath is orge.

Usage

"“The thing that David had done displeased the LORD” — one sentence after a chapter of scheming."

"“When the people complained, it displeased the LORD” — grumbling reckoned as sin."

"“He was much displeased… Suffer the little children” — the one occasion named of Christ."
